<description>
**Problem:** Block and undo writers buffer serialized data, then rely on the `BufferedWriter` destructor to write the remaining bytes.
`fwrite()` can report fewer bytes written than requested after a local storage error, e.g., if the filesystem fills up while a block is being written (my 1 TB benchmarking servers have recently been filling up, so I've been seeing these failures more often).
`AutoFile::write_buffer()` converts that result into an exception, and because the destructor is implicitly non-throwing, the exception invokes `std::terminate`.
Calling `flush()` before destruction is insufficient on its own because a failed flush leaves the same bytes pending, so the destructor retries the write while the original exception unwinds.

I introduced this bug in #31551 when adding `BufferedWriter`.

I’d update the **Fix** section to include `discard()` and describe exactly what the destructor checks. The problem statement and reproducer can stay as written.

**Fix:** Block and undo writers now flush explicitly before destruction.
If serialization or writing throws `std::ios_base::failure`, they discard any pending bytes, log the error, close the file, and request shutdown through the existing fatal-error path.
`BufferedWriter` clears the pending byte count before writing because the stream may obfuscate the bytes in place and a short write may already have put some of them on disk, making a retry unsafe.
The destructor uses `Assume` to check that no bytes are pending before attempting a fallback flush.
`flush()` continues to propagate exceptions, and `AutoFile` remains unchanged.

Manual write-error reproducer

Force the error path in `AutoFile::write_buffer()`:

```sh
sed -i '' '/^.*AutoFile::write_buffer(/,/^}/s/!= src.size()/!= 0/' src/streams.cpp
cmake -B build && cmake --build build -j5 && build/bin/bitcoind -regtest -datadir="$(mktemp -d)"; echo "exit=$?"
```

Before this change, implicit flushing invokes `std::terminate`:

[quoted text omitted]
With this change, `bitcoind` logs the write failure, then completes normal shutdown and exits with status 1:

[quoted text omitted]
</description>

[2026-11-17] rc:4605490959 inline on src/node/blockstorage.cpp by ryanofsky (member) (edited 2026-11-17):
In commit "blockstorage: handle buffered write failures" (1c33fa05dfe8a87444eebfdc0436d7cea3761600)

Could this catch `std::ios_base::failure` and call `fileout.discard()` (see the review summary), with `fileout` declared before the `try` so the `catch` can still call it?

As written, the cleanup here is only correct for exceptions thrown by `flush()`, which clears `m_buf_pos` before writing. `std::runtime_error` makes it look like any failure in the block is handled, but if anything else threw while bytes were still buffered, `~BufferedWriter` would run with data pending during unwinding, before this `catch` runs: the `Assume` would abort in debug builds, and release builds would write the failed block's partial data. Nothing else in the block throws right now, but nothing prevents other exceptions that would trigger the `Assume`. Adding a `discard()` call in the catch would make this actually exception-safe. Same in `WriteBlockUndo`.

[quoted text omitted]
An established pattern is the one this PR moves toward: destructors don't do work that can fail, and every object ends in an explicit call that reports success or failure, checked by an `Assume` in the destructor, as `AutoFile` does with `fclose()`. With a `discard()` method (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36049#pullrequestreview-5946234150), `BufferedWriter` would follow it too.

On a clang-tidy check: the existing [`bugprone-exception-escape`](https://clang.llvm.org/extra/clang-tidy/checks/bugprone/exception-escape.html) check, which flags destructors that can throw, doesn't catch this bug. It reports nothing for `~BufferedWriter` on master, probably because `AutoFile::write_buffer()` is defined in `streams.cpp`, where the check can't see that it throws. So it would probably need a custom `bitcoin-tidy` check.

A possible better alternative: throwing destructors, as in Cap'n Proto

Not something I'm suggesting for this PR, but another answer to the "wholesale" question: if `~BufferedWriter` were allowed to throw, RAII would just work. The destructor would flush automatically and report a write failure like any other error, so callers wouldn't need explicit `flush()` or `discard()` calls, and if the writer were destroyed because some other exception was already propagating, that original exception would take precedence instead of the program calling `std::terminate`.

This is how [Cap'n Proto](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/v2/style-guide.md#exceptions-can-happen-anywhere-including-destructors) handles it: destructors are declared `noexcept(false)`, and `kj::UnwindDetector` catches a destructor's failure only when another exception is already unwinding (the same rule as Java's try-with-resources). Both current callers would work this way, since each holds the writer as a local inside a `try` block.

The downside is that a throwing destructor is only safe when no `noexcept` code sits between it and the `catch`. Holding the writer in `std::unique_ptr`, `std::optional` or `std::vector`, or destroying it inside a `noexcept` function, would turn the error back into `std::terminate`, so making this fully safe would need a `bitcoin-tidy` check that flags those uses.
[2026-11-17] r:5946234150 review COMMENTED by ryanofsky (member):
Concept ACK 1c33fa05dfe8a87444eebfdc0436d7cea3761600. Turning the `std::terminate` on a failed block write into normal error handling is a clear improvement, but I think `BufferedWriter` needs a way to close without flushing.

The new `Assume(m_buf_pos == 0)` in the destructor means a writer can only be destroyed safely after a `flush()`. That assumes the only thing that can go wrong while writing is the flush itself, and that nothing else is ever a reason to stop without writing the buffered data, such as an exception from other code in the same scope or a caller abandoning the write (interrupt/shutdown). Right now the only way to empty the buffer on an error path is a flush that fails, which `flush()` handles by clearing `m_buf_pos` before it writes. `AutoFile` doesn't have this problem, because `fclose()` satisfies its `Assume` whether or not the close succeeds.

The `try`/`catch` blocks added to `WriteBlock` and `WriteBlockUndo` illustrate the problem (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36049#discussion_r4605490959): their cleanup is only correct because every exception in the block happens to come from `flush()`. A `discard()` method for error paths would mean every writer ends in an explicit `flush()` or `discard()`, with the destructor checking that, the same way `AutoFile` works.

```c++
    ~BufferedWriter()
    {
        Assume(m_buf_pos == 0); // Use explicit flush() or discard()
        flush();
    }

    //! Drop buffered bytes without writing them, e.g. after a write error.
    void discard() { m_buf_pos = 0; }
```
[2026-11-17] rc:4606185346 inline on src/streams.h by ryanofsky (member) (edited 2026-11-17):
In commit "streams: do not retry failed flushes" (a4199b39f92c3e572196f464a067f70b1d77cda5)

Note: It wasn't obvious to me why bytes were being discarded here. It looks like keeping them instead of discarding would be safer so a caller could retry, but a retry would write corrupt data: `AutoFile::write_buffer()` obfuscates the buffer in place before calling `fwrite()` and only advances its position after a successful write, so a second attempt would XOR the bytes again and write them unobfuscated. A short `fwrite()` can also leave part of the buffer already on disk. Maybe:

```suggestion
    //! Discard the buffered bytes even if writing them throws. After a failed
    //! write they can't be written again: the stream may have obfuscated them
    //! in place, and part of them may already be on disk.
```
